summary: This memo updates RFC 4733 by adding event codes for modem, fax and text telephony signals carried in the telephony event RTP payload. It supersedes the assignment of such codes in RFC 2833, obsoleting that part of it.

plainLanguage.summary:
A phone call that crosses the Internet is handled by a gateway at each end. When one side is a fax machine or a modem, the gateways must pass on the tones that control the connection, so the two devices can agree on a speed and start sending data. This RFC gives those tones numbered event codes, so one gateway can report a tone to the other over the same RTP stream that carries the call.

It also defines codes for the bits of the low-speed control channel, and for indicators that say what kind of modem or text terminal is on the line.

questions: what are rtp telephone events for fax and modem
what is the difference between v.8 and v.8 bis
subtitle: Event codes that let VoIP gateways report fax, modem and text-phone signals as small RTP events.

tldr.problem: When a phone call crosses the Internet, the gateways at each end must tell each other when a fax machine, a modem or a text terminal is starting, negotiating and finishing, so that the tones on the line can be reproduced for the equipment at the other end.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns numbered event codes to the tones, bit patterns and content indicators used by the ITU-T modem, fax and text start-up protocols, and says how each should be reported in the telephony event RTP payload defined in RFC 4733.
tldr.outcome: The codes supersede the assignment of such codes in RFC 2833, which this RFC therefore obsoletes, and they extend the telephony event registry established by RFC 4733.

facts.label: V.21 low channel
facts.value: 980 Hz for a '1' bit, 1180 Hz for a '0' bit

facts.label: V.21 high channel
facts.value: 1650 Hz for a '1' bit, 1850 Hz for a '0' bit

facts.label: Echo canceller reactivation
facts.value: As little as 100 ms of no signal on the line

today: RFC 4734 is a Proposed Standard from December 2006. It obsoletes RFC 2833, whose assignment of modem, fax and text telephony event codes it supersedes, and it updates RFC 4733 with the events it defines. Nothing has obsoleted it in turn.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC extends the set of telephony events defined in RFC 4733 to cover the control events and tones that can appear on a subscriber line serving a fax machine, a modem or a text telephony device. The events are organised into groups that match the ITU-T Recommendation in which each one is defined.

Their purpose is to support the negotiation, start-up and takedown of fax, modem and text telephony sessions, and the transitions between operating modes. The actual fax, modem and text payload is typically carried by other payload types, such as V.150.1 modem relay, voice-band data, Clearmode, T.38 for fax, or RFC 4103 for character-mode text.

The RFC states that implementers should not rely on its descriptions of the modem protocols without consulting the original ITU-T Recommendations. Those descriptions are given to provide context for the events, and they frequently omit details needed for an implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC names the tones a fax machine, a modem or a text terminal uses to start a call, and the small control messages they exchange. The names let a gateway pass those signals across the Internet.

sections.title: What the Events Are For
sections.content:
The typical application is a pair of gateways sitting between two terminals on the public switched telephone network, the PSTN, so that the Internet serves as a bridge between them. Each gateway acts as both sender and receiver.

Time constraints apply to the exchange of signals, which makes the early identification and reporting of events desirable so that receiver playout can proceed in a timely fashion. The receiver must play out events in their proper order, and the transfer of the events must be reliable, because applications vary in their ability to recover from missing events.

An implementation may simply ignore certain events, such as fax tones, that do not make sense in a particular environment. RFC 4733 specifies how the Session Description Protocol (SDP) "fmtp" parameter can be used to say which events an implementation is prepared to handle.

Echo suppressors and echo cancellers may re-activate after as little as 100 ms of no signal on the line. Where those devices must be disabled for signalling to work, tone events have to be reported quickly enough to ensure they do not become re-enabled. Buffering at the receiving end achieves continuity of playout, and a constant packetization interval at the sending end helps keep that buffering small.
sections.plainLanguage: Two gateways sit between the two ends of a phone call and pass signals between them. The signals have to arrive in order and on time, because the equipment at each end is waiting for them before it can start sending data.

sections.title: The Event Codes
sections.content:
Each event is reported under a numbered code in the telephony event payload. The codes defined here are added to the registry established by RFC 4733, and each registry entry names the signal and the Recommendation it comes from.

Most entries are tones. A tone event carries a frequency, a duration, a code and a flag saying whether the volume matters. The V.8 bis signals, for example, use a first segment of a dual-frequency tone held for 400 ms, which prepares the receiver and any in-line echo suppressor or canceller for what follows. The second segment follows immediately and is a single tone held for 100 ms, whose frequency identifies which of the six signals it is.

Other entries are indicators. An indicator says what kind of content the sender has detected on the line, such as V.21 modulation at 300 bits/s in the lower channel, or a Bell 103 class modem. The sender reports the initial event as soon as the nature of the audio content has been recognised, and retransmits it twice at short intervals, with 20 ms suggested, so that a lost packet does not lose the indicator.
sections.plainLanguage: Every signal gets a number. A gateway sends that number inside an RTP packet, and the gateway at the other end plays the tone out. Indicators work the same way, but they describe what kind of modem or text terminal is on the line.

sections.title: V.8 bis Signals
sections.content:
Recommendation V.8 bis is a general procedure for two endpoints to establish each other's capabilities and to transition between operating modes, both at call startup and after the call is established. It supports many of the same terminals as V.8 but allows more detailed parameter negotiation. It lacks support for some of the older V-series modems, but adds capabilities for simultaneous or alternating voice and data, H.324 multilink and T.120 conferencing.

V.8 bis distinguishes between signals and messages. The signals, ESi and ESr, MRd and MRe, CRd and CRe, consist of tones. The messages, MS, CL, CLR, ACK, NAK and NACK, consist of sequences of bits transported over V.21 modulation.

The complete ESi signal is represented by the event V8bISeg followed by ESiSeg, and the complete ESr by V8bRSeg followed by ESrSeg. The other second segments, CRdSeg, CReSeg, MRdSeg and MReSeg, follow either V8bISeg or V8bRSeg depending on context. ESiSeg and ESrSeg use the same frequencies as the V.21 low and high channel '1' bits, and are therefore assigned the same event codes.

No events are defined for the V.8 bis messages themselves. Applications may instead transfer the messages as sequences of bits using the V.21 bit events. If they do so, the transmitted information must include the complete contents of the message: the initial HDLC flags, the information field, the checksum and the terminating HDLC flags, together with the extra '0' bits added to prevent false recognition of HDLC flags at the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: V.8 bis is the start-up conversation two devices have before they send data. It announces what each side can do and agrees on the mode to use. This RFC names the tones used in that conversation so they can travel over the network.

sections.title: V.21 Bit Events
sections.content:
V.21 is a modem protocol offering data transmission at a maximum rate of 300 bits/s. Two channels are defined, supporting full duplex data transmission if required. The low channel uses frequencies 980 Hz for a '1' bit and 1180 Hz for a '0' bit; the high channel uses 1650 Hz for a '1' bit and 1850 Hz for a '0' bit. V.21 is used by other protocols, such as V.8 bis, V.18 and T.30, for the transmission of control data.

The RFC defines one event per bit. Sending implementations should report a completed event for every bit transmitted, rather than at transitions between '0' and '1'. Each event completion is transmitted three times, as the procedures of RFC 4733 require, which increases reporting redundancy, and RFC 2198 redundancy encoding is the recommended way to carry the retransmitted events in fewer packets. Eight to ten bits is a reasonable packetization interval.

One V.21 bit at the nominal rate of 300 bits/s lasts 3.33 ms, or 26.67 timestamp units at the default 8000 Hz sampling rate for the telephone-event payload. Because that duration is not a whole number of timestamp units, sending gateways should round the starting times of V.21 events to the nearest whole unit, and derive each event duration from the differences between consecutive starting times, so that the last event in one packet does not overlap the first event of the next.
sections.plainLanguage: Some control messages travel one bit at a time, at 300 bits per second. Each bit is sent as its own event and repeated three times, so a lost packet does not lose the message.

sections.title: Text Telephony and Modem Indicators
sections.content:
Legacy text telephony uses a wide variety of terminals, with different standards favoured in different parts of the world. Going forward, the vision is that new terminals work directly into the packet network and are based on RFC 4103 packetization of character data. In anticipation of this migration, the RFC recommends that text carried in the PSTN by legacy modem protocols be converted to RFC 4103 packets at the sending gateway.

During a transitional period, however, a gateway of lesser capability may recognise the nature of incoming content while being able to encode it only as voice-band data. The events in this section give the receiving end an indication of the nature of the voice-encoded data, so it can process the signal efficiently. They cover Baudot at 45.45 or 50 bits/s, EDT, which is V.21 at 110 bits/s in half-duplex mode, Bell 103 mode, V.23 based videotex in its Minitel and Prestel versions, and a non-V.18 text terminal using V.21 at 300 bits/s.

A final generic indicator, VBDGen, covers modem content for which no more specific event is available. It should not be sent when a more specific event exists.
sections.plainLanguage: Old text terminals use many different modems. A small event at the start of the audio tells the other end which one it is, so it can adjust its decoding. One generic event covers modems that nobody has a specific code for.

sections.title: Switching Payloads at the Gateway
sections.content:
The typical data application involves a pair of gateways interposed between two terminals on the PSTN. The gateways are likely to be serving a mixture of voice and data traffic, and need to adopt payload types appropriate to the media flows as they occur. If voice compression is in use for voice calls, the gateways need the flexibility to switch to other payload types when data streams are recognised.

Within the established IETF framework, the gateways must negotiate the potential payloads, voice, telephone-event, tones, voice-band data, T.38 fax and possibly RFC 4103 text and Clearmode octet streams, as separate payload types. From a timing point of view this is most easily done at the beginning of a call, but it results in an over-allocation of resources at the gateways and in the intervening network.

One alternative is to use named events to buy time while out-of-band signals are exchanged to update to the new payload type applicable to the session. Receiving gateways must be prepared to switch to the other payload type within the time constraints associated with the respective applications. A possible strategy is to send both the telephone-event and the data payload in an RFC 2198 redundancy arrangement, and for the receiving gateway to propagate the data payload whenever no event is in progress. For this to work, the data payload and the events must cover exactly the same content over the same time period, otherwise spurious events will be detected downstream.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway that carries both voice and data has to change the kind of data it sends as the call changes. Sending the tone events alongside the real data, using the redundancy format, lets the other end switch over at the right moment.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The V.21 bit events defined in this document may be used to transmit user-sensitive data. This could include initial log-on sequences and application-level protocol exchanges as well as user content. The attacks of concern are confidentiality violations and password sniffing, hijacking of data sessions through message insertion, modification of the transmitted content through man-in-the-middle attacks, and denial of service by means of message insertion, deletion and modification aimed at interference with the application protocol.

To prevent these attacks, the transmission of V.21 bit events must be given confidentiality protection. Message authentication and the protection of message integrity must also be provided. With these measures in place, RTP sequence numbers and the redundancy provided by the RFC 4733 procedures add protection against, and some resiliency in the face of, message deletion.

The other events defined in this document, and V.21 bit events within control sequences, are used only for the setup and control of sessions between data terminals or fax devices. Disclosure of these events would not expose user-sensitive data, but it can expose capabilities of the user equipment that could be exploited by attacks in the PSTN domain, so confidentiality protection should be provided. The primary threat is denial of service, through injection of inappropriate signals at vulnerable points in the control sequence or through alteration or blocking of enough event packets to disrupt that sequence.

The Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) meets the requirements for confidentiality, message integrity and message authentication described above. It should therefore be used to protect media streams containing the events described in this document, although the appropriate method of key distribution for SRTP may vary with the specific application.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these events carry log-on names and passwords, so the stream has to be encrypted and checked for tampering. The RFC recommends SRTP, the encrypted version of RTP, for that.

items.label: CRdSeg
items.desc: Second segment of the V.8 bis Capabilities Request signal.

items.label: CReSeg
items.desc: Second segment of the V.8 bis Capabilities Request signal from an automatic answering terminal.

items.label: MRdSeg
items.desc: Second segment of the V.8 bis Mode Request signal.

items.label: MReSeg
items.desc: Second segment of the V.8 bis Mode Request signal from an automatic answering terminal.

items.label: V32AC
items.desc: The answering pattern of a V.32/V.32bis terminal, modulated at 4800 bits/s.

items.label: V8bISeg
items.desc: First segment of an initiating V.8 bis signal: a dual-frequency tone held for 400 ms.

items.label: V8bRSeg
items.desc: First segment of a responding V.8 bis signal: a dual-frequency tone held for 400 ms.

items.label: ANS
items.desc: The V.25 answer tone, also known as the T.30 called tone.

items.label: /ANS
items.desc: The V.25 answer tone after a phase shift.

items.label: ANSam
items.desc: The V.8 amplitude modified answer tone.

items.label: /ANSam
items.desc: The V.8 amplitude modified answer tone after a phase shift.

items.label: CNG
items.desc: The T.30 calling tone, sent by the calling fax terminal.

items.label: V.21 channel 1, '0' bit
items.desc: 1180 Hz on the low channel.

items.label: V.21 channel 1, '1' bit
items.desc: 980 Hz on the low channel; also used for ESiSeg.

items.label: V.21 channel 2, '0' bit
items.desc: 1850 Hz on the high channel.

items.label: V.21 channel 2, '1' bit
items.desc: 1650 Hz on the high channel; also used for ESrSeg.

items.label: CT
items.desc: The V.25 calling tone.

items.label: ANS2225
items.desc: A 2225 Hz answer tone detected, an indication for text telephony.

items.label: CI
items.desc: The V.8 call indicator signal preamble.

items.label: V21L110
items.desc: V.21 modulation at 110 bits/s in the lower channel, for text telephony.

items.label: B103L300
items.desc: Bell 103 class modulation in the low channel at 300 bits/s.

items.label: VBDGen
items.desc: Tone patterns indicating an unidentified modem type.

items.label: XCIMark
items.desc: A pattern of bits modulated in the V.23 main channel by a V.18 calling terminal.

items.label: V32AA
items.desc: The calling pattern of a V.32/V.32bis terminal, modulated at 4800 bits/s.

messages.label: ANSam event
messages.note: At 250.0 ms the called gateway sends the first ANSam event packet. The calling gateway starts playout when the report arrives.

messages.label: CM bits
messages.note: At 1325.0 ms the calling gateway sends a packet containing the first 9 bits of the call menu signal.

messages.label: JM bits
messages.note: At 1660.0 ms the called gateway sends the final /ANSam report together with the first 7 bits of the joint menu signal.

messages.label: CJ bits
messages.note: At 2015.0 ms the calling gateway sends the final 3 bits of the call menu signal and the first 6 bits of the CM terminator.

messages.label: V.34 voice-band data
messages.note: At 2195.0 ms the calling gateway sends a first packet of V.34 signalling as voice-band data in PCMU.
